answer: DeepWalk tends to outperform standard classification methods that predict labels directly from the graph (such as relational/collective classifiers operating on the adjacency structure or neighborhood label propagation) when the graph is only partially labeled and the labels are correlated with network community structure (homophily), so that learned latent node representations capture the graph's structure in a way that generalizes to unlabeled nodes. Its advantage is greatest when labeled data is sparse (few labeled nodes per class), since the unsupervised embeddings are learned from random walks over the whole graph and then fed to a simple classifier (e.g., logistic regression), making it robust to sparse labels and able to capture higher-order, indirect neighborhood relationships rather than relying only on direct neighbors' labels. Conversely, when the graph is dense with abundant labels or the labels are not well aligned with graph structure, direct graph-based classifiers can match or outperform it. In the original DeepWalk evaluation (Perozzi et al., 2014) on BlogCatalog, Flickr, and YouTube, DeepWalk remained competitive or superior especially when the fraction of labeled nodes was small, while being scalable and parallelizable.
